model.title: How does the writer use language and structure to show what the climb meant to her?

parts.text: Language: the counting 'twenty, then rest' mirrors her laboured breathing
Effect: the reader feels the effort in the rhythm
Structure: the anticlimax of 'only cloud' then the turn 'And yet'
Effect: the meaning shifts from the view to the achievement: 'I had earned the silence'

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: The counted rhythm of 'twenty, then rest' makes us feel her effort, and the structural turn from the anticlimax of 'only cloud' to 'And yet' shifts the meaning from the view to the achievement: she 'had earned the silence'.

model.title: Compare how the two writers present reaching the top

parts.text: Similarity: both find the summit is not what they expected
Text One: 'only cloud, thick and white as wool', met with laughter
Text Two: the valley 'like a map unrolled', met with tears
Difference in perspective: quiet pride versus overwhelmed awe, admitted reluctantly

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: Both writers find the summit unexpected, but whereas the modern writer laughs at 'only cloud' and feels quiet pride, the letter-writer, faced with a valley 'like a map unrolled', weeps, an awe he will 'deny' to his brother.

questions.q: Write a comparative sentence using 'whereas' about the two writers' feelings
questions.a: For example: Whereas the first writer laughs, the second weeps.

questions.q: Core: DIRT: rewrite one Q7 paragraph so it compares in every sentence
Extend: improve your weaker 10-mark answer (Q3 or Q6) using the model
Stretch: write two Section A targets for the mock
questions.a: For example: compare in every Q7 sentence; explain one effect per quotation

questions.q: What most often holds Q7 back?
options: writing about one text, then the other, without comparing
questions.a: A) writing about one text, then the other, without comparing. Q7 rewards comparison in every paragraph, not two separate essays.
